Service & Product
Design for Takumi

A two-sided influencer marketing platform connecting global brands with creators and their agencies. Three user groups. Two disconnected products. One strategic question unanswered.

Role
Service & Product Designer
Clients
La Roche-Posay, Max Factor
Methods
Service mapping · Workshops · Research · Ops shadowing
Designer
Ashimi Adefesobi
The brief

Two stakeholders.
Two directions to reconcile.

I was brought in by Dmitry, one of the founders, to answer a strategic question before a single screen was touched. Marco, the CEO, had a competing concept he believed would differentiate the product.

Dmitry · Co-founder

Strategic prioritisation

"We don't know what product we should start on, or which user we should be prioritising first."

Wanted evidence-based direction. Open brief. Direction not yet decided.

Brief: open. Evidence needed first.
Marco · CEO

InfluenScore concept

A composite scoring system to surface the best-matched creators for each campaign and differentiate Takumi from competitors.

Legitimate concept — but a single fixed score risked flattening what different clients actually value.

Needed a path that worked for both.
Discovery

Map the whole service before picking anywhere to start.

The first step was a workshop with the team to map the full campaign lifecycle — from brand brief through influencer selection, content creation, approval, and payment. This made visible what no single team could see from inside.

The ops team were bridging gaps that the platform should have been handling. There were manual handoffs, unclear ownership, and places where client confidence in the process was low.

From this I developed a full 16-phase service blueprint across five swim lanes — brand client, influencer, influencer agent, client-facing staff, and support systems. The map surfaced a clear pressure point: the shortlisting stage, where all three user groups intersected. It was where escalations started and where approvals stalled.

The shortlist became the answer to Dmitry's question — not because of intuition, but because the map showed it was the one place where fixing a single thing would lift the experience for all three user groups at once.

The problem — before

A flat table where a decision-making tool should have been.

Watching brand clients use the existing shortlist made the problems immediately visible. They were scrolling back and forth between profiles, struggling to compare, and when they rejected a creator the process stalled entirely.

No comparison possible

Clients flicking between profiles with no side-by-side view. No way to evaluate creators against each other at a glance.

Rejection stalled the process

Reject a creator → back to ops. No recovery path in the platform. Every rejection became a manual intervention.

Approval outside the platform

Feedback via email and Slack. No shared record of what had been approved, requested for revision, or rejected.

Current / previous design — Brand match interface Before
The redesign — InfluenSelect

Started as a reskin.
The evidence made the case for a redesign.

The shortlist was originally scoped as a visual refresh. But clients weren't struggling because of how it looked — they were struggling because comparison was hard and rejection had no recovery. A reskin would not have fixed either of those things.

The visual direction was deliberately Spotify-inspired: dark mode to let creator content lead, card-based browsing to make a curated list feel trustworthy, editorial treatment of creator profiles rather than rows in a database.

Campaign context + curator attribution

Brand name, campaign, and curator shown at the top. Gives brands confidence in what they're reviewing before they look at a single creator.

Rich creator profiles with side panel

Per-platform stats, engagement rate, audience tags, bio. Key information at a glance on the card — fuller detail available on click, not forced into every row.

Reject + immediate alternative surfaced

Rejecting a creator instantly surfaces a replacement. The approval process keeps moving without reverting to ops.

InfluenScore — weighted and configurable

A composite score per creator in the Recommended section, shaped by what a given campaign cares about — not a fixed top-down definition. Marco's concept, grounded in how clients actually use it.

Key design decisions

The judgement calls that shaped the work.

Decision 01

Sequencing the shortlist and InfluenScore

Rather than choosing one stakeholder's priority over the other, I proposed sequencing. The shortlist first — that was where pain was biggest and where one fix lifted all three user groups. InfluenScore into research and prototyping in parallel, so when the time came to build it, the design would be grounded in evidence rather than assumption.

Both stakeholders got a yes. Neither got their yes at the expense of the other.
Shortlist — now
→
InfluenScore — parallel
Decision 02

Reskin versus redesign

The shortlist was scoped as a visual refresh. But clients weren't struggling because of how it looked. They were struggling because comparison was hard and rejection had no recovery. A reskin would not have fixed either.

I made the case to expand the scope, and was deliberate about what that meant in practice.

  • Side-by-side creator comparison
  • Key metrics at a glance
  • Immediate alternative on rejection
  • Fuller detail on click — card kept clean
Outcome

What the engagement delivered.

Strategic clarity

The service map gave the team a shared view of their operation that had never been written down. People started referring to it in meetings rather than re-describing the problem from scratch each time.

Launched shortlist and decision workspace

Launched an in-platform shortlist and decision workspace during the engagement, replacing off-platform spreadsheets and workbooks. Selection, comparison, ranked alternatives, InfluenScore and running budget totals supported the decision.

InfluenScore direction

Research synthesis and prototype framework ready to continue — direction set for a weighted, configurable model shaped by how clients actually use it, not a fixed top-down score.

Documentation standards

Shared documentation introduced across product, engineering and ops. Decisions and rationale recorded as the work progressed — handover-ready from day one.

The shortlist and decision workspace launched during the engagement. No usability issues were reported after launch, and some clients expressed delight with its ease of use. This is qualitative feedback, without a measured usability result. The wider service redesign was not fully delivered before the engagement ended as the business prepared for acquisition. The screens shown here illustrate the design work; they do not establish that every proposed interaction shipped unchanged.
Reflection

What I took from it.

01

Ambiguity as a brief

Dmitry hired me with an honest version of the problem: we don't know. That is the easiest kind of brief to work with — the answer is not pre-decided and you get to earn the direction rather than justify it.

02

Service mapping as a forcing function for prioritisation

It is tempting to answer where should we start with intuition. The map let me answer it with evidence — it showed which pain point sat at the intersection of the most user groups. That is a pattern worth repeating.

03

Scope management is a design skill

The shortlist work started as a reskin and needed to become something bigger — but not everything bigger. Knowing which expansion to fight for and which to defer is where the design judgement actually lives.

04

Design handover-ready from day one

The acquisition context meant priorities shifted fast. Clear rationale and documented decisions meant the work could continue under whoever picked it up, without me in the room to explain it.
